reading.s: Serotonin syndrome comes from too much serotonin, so I'd stop anything suspected of adding more (serotonergic substances).
reading.why: the reason first, then what to do, the term after its plain words, as in your step 5

reading.s: No more MDMA or other stimulants, of course, but also no DXM cough syrup, the painkiller tramadol or the antibiotic linezolid.
reading.why: the obvious ones first, then "but also" the ones people don't think of, each said with what it is

reading.s: Even if they take an antidepressant every day (an SSRI like Prozac, or an SNRI or MAOI), I'd skip it until a doctor says to restart it, since missing a dose is much less risky than more serotonin right now.
reading.why: it answers the reader's worry about stopping a daily medicine, but the bracket of kinds may read like a list dropped in

reading.s: If they drank ayahuasca or another harmala brew, like Syrian rue, no more of that either, since those work the way MAOIs do.
reading.why: it starts from what the reader may be facing (they drank ayahuasca), then what to do and why

reading.s: And check whether they take supplements people don't think of as drugs, like 5-HTP, St John's wort or SAM-e.
reading.why: something to do, ending on what's in their own cupboard

reading.s: When you call medics, ask for an ambulance, since the person can get worse fast, with seizures or dangerous overheating.
reading.why: the act the line before asked for, with why an ambulance

reading.s: It may seem faster to drive them to the ER yourself, but don't: paramedics can start treating them right there, and if they have a seizure in your car, you can't help them and drive at the same time.
reading.why: the urge first (it may seem faster), then what can actually happen, pictured (a seizure in your car)

reading.s: Poison control can't treat serotonin syndrome, but if you don't know what was mixed, they can help work that out once the ambulance is on its way.
reading.why: the limit comes first ("can't treat"), which may read as a correction before the help it gives

reading.s: Their twitching and tense muscles are making a lot of heat, and overheating is the most dangerous part of serotonin syndrome, so while you wait for the ambulance, I'd get them somewhere cool, take off their extra clothes, and set a fan blowing over cool damp cloths on their skin.
reading.why: the reason and three acts in one long sentence; I joined them your way, but it may read packed

reading.s: If they still feel hot, ice packs wrapped in cloth help most at the neck, armpits and groin.
reading.why: the next step only if needed, with where the packs help most

reading.s: A cold bath would cool them faster, but if they're confused, seizing or very weak, they could slip under or breathe in water, so don't put them in one.
reading.why: it argues the rule in three clauses (would, but if, so don't), and that build read AI in the last check

reading.s: And don't count on fever reducers like Tylenol or ibuprofen, which do not help with heat generated by muscles.
reading.why: what the reader reaches for, and why it won't work, in one plain line

reading.s: The ER doctors will want to know exactly what they took, so before the ambulance comes, I'd gather their pill bottles and packages.
reading.why: why first (the ER doctors will want to know), then the act

reading.s: I'd also jot down how much of each and when, street drugs and supplements included.
reading.why: the next thing to write down, in plain words ("jot down", "street drugs")

reading.s: If they raised the dose of anything lately, note that too, since a bigger dose alone can set off serotonin syndrome.
reading.why: one detail to note, with why it matters

reading.s: And if you have a thermometer or a blood pressure cuff, take readings every so often and write them down with the time, so the doctors can see whether things are getting better or worse.
reading.why: what they can measure with what they may have at home, and what the doctors get from it

reading.s: If you do get it, I'd give an adult 12 mg to start, and tell the medics you did.
reading.why: "If you do get it" ties it to the line before and the dose comes at once, but "to start" leaves the next doses unsaid (I left those to the medics, since the ambulance comes long before two hours)

reading.s: If they still show the signs of low electrolytes from MDMA: Magnesium Alarm above, they may need a hypertonic electrolyte drink with more salt and magnesium than a normal one.
reading.why: "still" ties it to the sips, and the drink, in your bold, comes as soon as the condition is said; the signs stay in your MDMA section, as you asked, so the reader follows the link

reading.s: That can be as simple as a pinch of salt and some magnesium chloride flakes stirred into an ordinary one, or a salty broth with the flakes in it.
reading.why: your "as simple as" and what a kitchen has, but "some" flakes is no amount, and the amounts your MDMA section gives are for jaw tension, not a drink

reading.s: And while you might think to add potassium too, since it can run low after MDMA, I wouldn't add any, because muscles breaking down into the blood release a lot of it, and too much can stop the heart.
reading.why: your "And while you might think" names the urge before the don't, and the reason comes from step 5, but it carries two reasons (since, because) and may be one too many

reading.s: And if they have a seizure while you wait, do the first aid in Active Seizure above.
reading.why: "while you wait" ties it to the step, and it points to your first aid instead of saying it again

reading.s: Then I'd tell the medics whether their breathing got better or worse afterward, since the CDC counts trouble breathing after a seizure as a danger sign.
reading.why: your act and your reason in your order ("make note if their breathing is getting better or worse"), with the seizure now one they had and who the note is for

reading.s: Slow, shallow breathing can mean an opioid overdose, which naloxone reverses, so if you have it (the Narcan nasal spray), spray it into one nostril right away.
reading.why: the reason first, as in your steps, but three things come before the act (what it may be, what reverses it, the brand in brackets)

reading.s: It doesn't matter if they think they only took MDMA, since fentanyl, an opioid, has turned up in pills sold as MDMA, and naloxone does no harm without one.
reading.why: your "It doesn't matter if" answers the doubt the reader will have, then both reasons to give it anyway

reading.s: But naloxone can wear off before the opioid does, so call medics even if they wake up, and if their breathing slows again before help comes, give the second spray in the pack.
reading.why: "But" ties it, and each act follows from the wearing off, but two acts in one sentence, the second with its own condition

reading.s: But if they feel a strong urge to keep moving (akathisia), I'd have them tap their fingertips on their head instead (the Emotional Freedom Technique), which can soothe that urge without the over-activity risk.
reading.why: "instead" ties it to the pacing just ruled out, and each term comes after its plain words, but two asides in brackets in one sentence may read like terms dropped in

reading.s: That can be as simple as a salty potato broth with some magnesium chloride flakes stirred in, since potatoes are full of potassium.
reading.why: "That" ties it and the broth comes first, your idea with its reason, but a reader waiting for an ambulance may not have time to cook potatoes, and "some" is still no amount

reading.s: If you don't have the flakes, Epsom salt works too, although it causes diarrhea more easily.
reading.why: the tie at the start answers what the reader will ask next, then your trade-off in your words

reading.s: Whatever you give, give it slowly to see how it affects them, since their potassium could be running low or high: MDMA can drain it, but muscles breaking down into the blood can push it up.
reading.why: the act comes first, your "slowly", and the reason says which way potassium goes, as you asked, but the colon packs both directions after the act

reading.s: So I'd stick to food like the potato broth for potassium, since too much pure potassium is dangerous for anyone.
reading.why: "So" ties it to the line before, the act first, and the reason is the one you gave

reading.s: DMSO, though, seems to help prevent seizures, so if there's any sign of an overdose, I'd start by having them smell it, or rub a little on a clean patch of skin, mixed with about 30% water if it makes the skin itch.
reading.why: "though" ties it to niacin and the reason comes first, your order, but the sentence carries a condition and two ways to give it with a third condition on the second

reading.s: Then I'd use more, a little at a time, as long as it seems to help, since seizures have happened when a lot of DMSO went straight into the blood with stem cell infusions.
reading.why: "Then" ties it, but the reason is a hospital case far from a skin rub, and the reader has to work out why it means going slowly

reading.s: Magnesium chloride is the other one I'd use, since many people with serotonin syndrome run low on magnesium.
reading.why: "the other one" ties it to DMSO, your line with the one word that changed

reading.s: If they're not able to swallow, I'd rub magnesium chloride on their skin instead, dissolved in a little water, or Epsom salt if that's all you have, though Epsom salt gets through the skin less well.
reading.why: the condition is the reader's case and the act comes right after it, but three additions follow the act

reading.s: Women are most at risk of this: at one rave, about one in four women who took MDMA had low sodium, against 3% of men.
reading.why: "of this" ties it to the low sodium just named, the claim first and then the numbers that show it

reading.s: To tell whether too much water is the problem, ask whether they've drunk a lot, and look for bloating, puffy hands, or rings that feel tight.
reading.why: the purpose opens the sentence, which says why to read on, but it delays the act by eight words
